unit.title: Mathematical Modelling Capstone
unit.essential_question: How can mathematics be used responsibly to define a problem, build and test a model, make a limited recommendation, and communicate what the evidence can—and cannot—support?
big_ideas: Modelling begins with a meaningful, safe, and answerable question.
Variables, units, representations, and assumptions must be defined before calculation.
Models improve through verification, validation, revision, and sensitivity testing.
Uncertainty, fairness, accessibility, privacy, and limitations are part of mathematical quality.
A defensible conclusion connects claim, evidence, reasoning, assumptions, and limits.
Reflection on modelling practices supports transition into Algebra I.
unit.architecture: Open-age mathematical modelling capstone: frame a meaningful/safe/answerable question + define variables/units/data + select representations + build/calculate/verify/revise + test assumptions/sensitivity/uncertainty/fairness + communicate/defend/reflect + Algebra I readiness
unit.tool_integration: Calculator, graphing/data tools, geometry/CAD resources, handwriting/tracing, simulations, Evidence Citation Studio, and approved tools may support work while students retain an audit trail.
unit.capstone_gate: NAIB may summarize readiness strengths, gaps, and suggested supports. Placement remains a parent/guardian decision.
unit.readiness_note: Unit 13 is an open-age capstone. It measures transfer, modelling judgment, communication, and Algebra I readiness through demonstrated evidence rather than grade identity.

lessons.title: Frame a Meaningful, Safe & Answerable Question
objectives: Choose a meaningful modelling context.
Write a focused, answerable question.
Identify audience, purpose, privacy, ethics, and success criteria.
Distinguish observations, decisions, predictions, and recommendations.
warmup: Which question is narrow enough to investigate in one week?
Name one stakeholder affected by a school or community decision.
Explain why a useful model may still have limits.

concepts.heading: Start with a decision, not a formula
concepts.body: A strong model begins with a purpose, audience, and question that mathematics can inform.

concepts.heading: Scope protects quality
concepts.body: A focused question defines who, what, where, and when without collecting unnecessary personal information.

concepts.heading: Success criteria guide the work
concepts.body: Criteria describe what a useful answer must include, such as cost, capacity, fairness, time, or uncertainty.

examples.problem: Improve “How can our community be better?”
steps: Set a time frame and audience.
examples.answer: Which of three fictional park-cleanup schedules removes the most waste per volunteer-hour within a $600 budget?

examples.problem: Protect privacy in a travel-time study.
steps: Use broad zones or fictional routes.
Collect only variables needed for the question.
examples.answer: Record anonymous travel minutes and transport mode, not identities or home locations.

examples.problem: Define success for a water-use plan.
examples.answer: Reduce projected use by at least 15% without exceeding the maintenance budget or excluding high-need users.

pathways.Foundation: Use a question frame, stakeholder map, and checklist for safe scope.
pathways.Core: Write a focused question with purpose, audience, criteria, constraints, and privacy choices.
pathways.Extended: Compare competing objectives, ethical trade-offs, feasibility, and unintended consequences.

lessons.application: Draft a safe capstone question from an environmental, artistic, financial, scientific, educational, design, or civic context using public, fictional, aggregated, or anonymous information.

questions.prompt: Which is most answerable in one week?
options: Which of three fictional garden layouts provides the most planting area under a 24 m fence limit?
questions.explanation: It defines alternatives, a measurable outcome, and a constraint.

questions.prompt: The purpose of a model should state:
options: the decision or understanding the model will support
questions.explanation: Purpose connects mathematics to a real decision or explanation.

options: study every city in the world
define one school term, one population, and two measurable outcomes
questions.explanation: Boundaries make the investigation feasible and interpretable.

options: require medical histories for a transport study
collect only information needed for the question
questions.explanation: Data minimization reduces unnecessary risk.

options: a measurable condition used to judge a solution
questions.explanation: Criteria make evaluation transparent.

lessons.title: Select Variables, Mathematics, Data & Representations
objectives: Define variables, units, sources, and assumptions.
Choose mathematics from across the course.
Match tables, graphs, equations, geometry, and statistics to the question.
Create a model plan before calculating.
warmup: Name the units for cost, time, area, and rate.
Choose a graph for a relationship that changes over time.

concepts.heading: Variables need names, meanings, and units
concepts.body: Clear definitions prevent symbols and measurements from changing meaning during the investigation.

concepts.heading: Representations should answer the question
concepts.body: Tables organize cases, graphs reveal patterns, equations generalize relationships, and geometry models space.

concepts.heading: Use more than one mathematical lens
concepts.body: A strong capstone often connects number, algebra, geometry, statistics, probability, or financial reasoning.

steps: Define wall area and coverage rate.
Include paint cost and waste allowance.
examples.answer: Litres needed = area ÷ coverage, adjusted by a stated waste factor; compare costs in a table.
Revenue R=pa with 0≤a≤capacity; graph scenarios and compare assumptions.
A sourced dataset is usable only after its variables and collection method are understood.

pathways.Foundation: Use a variable-and-unit table plus a representation chooser.
pathways.Core: Define variables, select at least three connected representations, and justify each choice.
pathways.Extended: Compare alternative models, parameter choices, transformations, and data-source quality.

lessons.application: Create a model plan listing variables, units, data or fictional inputs, assumptions, formulas or procedures, and at least three connected representations.

questions.explanation: A reader must know what the variable measures and in what unit.

questions.prompt: Best representation for comparing several scenarios across cost and benefit:
questions.explanation: A table supports systematic comparison.

questions.prompt: A room can hold at most 120 people. This is represented by:
questions.explanation: At most means less than or equal to.
Source transparency supports evaluation.

questions.prompt: A strong capstone model may combine:
options: algebra, geometry, statistics, probability, or finance as appropriate
questions.explanation: The mathematics should fit the problem and connect representations.

lessons.title: Build, Calculate, Verify & Revise the Model
objectives: Carry out calculations accurately with units.
Check results using estimation, inverse operations, alternate representations, or technology.
Identify errors and revise the model.
Document a reproducible method.
warmup: Name two ways to verify a percentage calculation.
Explain why units can expose an error.

concepts.heading: A model is a process, not one answer
concepts.body: Building includes defining, calculating, checking, revising, and recording enough detail for another person to follow.

concepts.heading: Verification uses independent checks
concepts.body: Estimate, substitute back, use another representation, inspect units, or recalculate with a different method.

concepts.heading: Revision is evidence of quality
concepts.body: Finding a flaw and improving the model is stronger than hiding an error.

examples.answer: A consistent scale factor should reproduce every corresponding length.

steps: Compute the change and divide by original.
Reverse by multiplying the original by 1+rate.
examples.answer: The forward and reverse calculations should agree apart from stated rounding.

steps: Identify where the pattern may stop.
Restrict the domain or choose another model.
examples.answer: A model should not be extended beyond the range where its assumptions remain reasonable.

pathways.Foundation: Use a calculation log with estimate, work, units, and check columns.
pathways.Core: Verify every major result with at least one independent method and revise documented errors.
pathways.Extended: Compare model forms, residuals, numerical sensitivity, and validation evidence.

lessons.application: Build the first complete version of the model, showing formulas, substitutions, units, calculations, representations, verification checks, and revisions.

questions.prompt: Estimating before an exact calculation helps:
questions.explanation: A rough expected range can reveal entry or operation errors.

questions.prompt: If a formula for area produces metres rather than square metres, the model likely has:
questions.explanation: Area requires squared length units.

questions.prompt: Which is an independent check for solving an equation?
options: substitute the solution into the original equation
questions.explanation: Substitution tests whether the original relationship is satisfied.

options: keep reasonable precision and round the final result as context requires
questions.explanation: Early rounding can accumulate error.

questions.prompt: When a model predicts an impossible value, first:
options: inspect assumptions, domain, data, and calculations
questions.explanation: Impossible output signals a need to diagnose and revise.

lessons.title: Test Assumptions, Sensitivity, Uncertainty & Fairness
objectives: Identify assumptions and limitations.
Test how outputs change when inputs change.
Use scenarios, intervals, probability, or error measures to communicate uncertainty.
Evaluate fairness, accessibility, and unintended consequences.
warmup: Change one input by 10% and predict the output direction.
Name an assumption that could fail in a budget model.
Explain why a mathematically optimal plan may be unfair.

concepts.heading: Assumptions are part of the model
concepts.body: Every model simplifies reality; assumptions should be explicit and tested rather than hidden.

concepts.heading: Sensitivity reveals influential inputs
concepts.body: Change one input at a time or compare scenarios to see which assumptions drive the conclusion.

concepts.heading: A decision can be accurate but harmful
concepts.body: Fairness, accessibility, privacy, and unequal effects belong in model evaluation.

steps: Set low, baseline, and high attendance.
examples.answer: A robust recommendation remains reasonable across plausible attendance scenarios.

steps: Use a plausible range for daily waste.
Calculate weekly totals at both ends.
State the interval rather than false precision.
examples.answer: Report a range supported by the input uncertainty.

examples.problem: Evaluate fairness in a route plan.
steps: Check the longest times and affected groups.
examples.answer: A lower average alone may not justify disproportionate burdens on one group.

pathways.Foundation: Use low, middle, and high scenarios with a guided limitations list.
pathways.Core: Run sensitivity tests, communicate uncertainty, and evaluate fairness and access.
pathways.Extended: Analyze robustness, trade-offs, risk, distributional effects, and alternative objectives.

lessons.application: Test at least three plausible scenarios, identify the most influential assumption, describe uncertainty, and evaluate who benefits, who may be burdened, and what the model misses.

options: a condition accepted for the model that may need testing
questions.explanation: Assumptions simplify or define how the model works.

options: how output changes when an input or assumption changes
questions.explanation: It identifies influential inputs and robustness.

options: the most dramatic possible case only
a reasonable central set of stated assumptions
questions.explanation: The baseline is the main comparison case.

questions.prompt: A recommendation is robust when it:
options: depends on one exact input only
questions.explanation: Robust conclusions are not fragile to small changes.

options: how effects differ across people or groups, including access and burdens
questions.explanation: Distributional effects can be hidden by averages.

lessons.title: Communicate, Defend, Reflect & Demonstrate Readiness
objectives: Write a conclusion proportional to the evidence.
Present connected representations clearly.
Respond to questions and defend choices without overstating certainty.
Reflect on growth and Algebra I readiness.
warmup: Rewrite an absolute claim with appropriate uncertainty.
Name one graph feature that helps accessibility.
Explain the difference between defending a method and refusing criticism.

concepts.heading: Conclusions must match the evidence
concepts.body: State what the model supports, under which assumptions, and what it cannot establish.

concepts.heading: Defence means transparent reasoning
concepts.body: A strong defence explains choices, acknowledges limitations, and revises when a critique is valid.

concepts.heading: Reflection converts a project into readiness
concepts.body: Learners identify transferable strengths, unfinished skills, and next steps for Algebra I.

examples.answer: Under the baseline cost and attendance assumptions, Option A has the lowest projected cost per participant; the ranking changes if attendance falls below 60.
Explain why the representation was chosen and what additional data would strengthen the conclusion.
I can connect tables, graphs, and equations; I need more practice isolating variables, so I will complete two formula-rearrangement reviews.

pathways.Foundation: Use a presentation frame, caption checklist, and guided reflection prompts.
pathways.Core: Present a clear claim-evidence-reasoning chain and complete a short defence.
pathways.Extended: Address counterarguments, compare alternative models, and propose future research.

lessons.application: Complete the capstone portfolio, present a three-to-five-minute defence, respond to questions, revise one element from feedback, and complete the Algebra I readiness reflection.

options: match the evidence and state assumptions and limits
questions.explanation: The strength of the claim should not exceed the evidence.

options: what is shown and the main interpretation in context
questions.explanation: Captions help readers interpret the representation.

questions.prompt: During a defence, a valid critique should be:
options: treated as proof the entire project failed
considered and used to clarify or revise the model
questions.explanation: Revision in response to evidence is a modelling strength.

options: specific strengths, challenges, evidence of growth, and next steps
questions.explanation: Specific reflection supports future learning.

questions.prompt: Algebra I readiness includes the ability to:
options: connect quantities, variables, tables, graphs, equations, and constraints
questions.explanation: Algebra builds on connected representations and reasoning.
